title: Devlens Research Summary: Bangladeshis top sea arrivals to Italy
excerpt: Mixed Migration Review 2026: Bangladeshis were 29.5% of sea arrivals in Italy in early 2026, and Rohingya sea deaths hit 820 in six months.
content:
DHAKA, 28 November 2026: Bangladeshis were the largest single nationality reaching Italy by sea in the first half of 2026, making up 29.5% of arrivals, and the largest on the Eastern Mediterranean route to Greece, at 29.1%, according to the Mixed Migration Review 2026, published by the Mixed Migration Centre (MMC) and posted on ReliefWeb on Thursday (26 November). The same report finds that the Bay of Bengal and Andaman Sea route used by Rohingya refugees recorded 820 deaths and disappearances in the first six months of 2026, close to the 860 recorded in the whole of 2025.

The 272-page global yearbook covers Bangladesh twice: as a main country of origin for irregular migration to Europe, and as host to about 1.2 million Rohingya refugees whose aid is shrinking.

The source

Mixed Migration Review 2026: Migration in the age of polycrisis, edited by Jennifer Vallentine and Bram Frouws of the MMC, which is part of the Danish Refugee Council. Most of its figures are compiled from other sources, mainly UNHCR, the International Organization for Migration (IOM), Frontex and the EU Agency for Asylum, plus the MMC's own 4Mi surveys of people on the move. It is an analysis, not a new survey of Bangladesh. Devlens has read the Bangladesh and Rohingya sections of the full PDF. Where useful, this summary adds figures from UNHCR's Routes Monitor key updates for November 2026, also published on 26 November.

Where things stand

Irregular arrivals in Europe fell sharply in 2026. Sea arrivals in Italy dropped 55% in the first seven months, to 16,567 from 36,545 in the same period of 2025. Arrivals in Greece fell to 19,506 in the same seven months, 25% lower than a year earlier. But the routes became deadlier: the Central Mediterranean recorded 872 deaths or disappearances in the first seven months of 2026, against 623 a year earlier, almost half of them in January during Cyclone Harry.

Finding 1: Bangladeshis lead both Mediterranean routes

In the first half of 2026, Bangladeshis made up 29.5% of sea arrivals in Italy, ahead of Somalis (11.4%), Sudanese (9.5%) and Pakistanis (8.2%). Libya was the departure point for 80.7% of arrivals in Italy. On the Eastern Mediterranean route, Bangladesh (29.1%) and Sudan (28.4%) were the top countries of origin, and the report says their share grew "due in large part to the growing prominence of the North Africa route from Libya" to Crete. UNHCR's monthly update shows the mix shifting: in September 2026 arrivals in Italy were led by Algerians, Eritreans, Bangladeshis and Somalis, while in September 2025 Bangladeshis and Egyptians predominated.

Finding 2: Legal migration often comes first

The review says Bangladesh "illustrates" a mismatch between migration rules and reality. In 2025 Bangladeshis were the fourth-largest nationality applying for asylum in the European Union, despite a first-instance recognition rate of only about 3% and Bangladesh's inclusion on the EU's proposed list of safe countries of origin. Citing earlier MMC research on the route to Italy through Libya, it says many Bangladeshi migrants first pursue legal labour migration before being redirected into irregular routes.

Finding 3: The Rohingya sea route is now one of the deadliest

Using UNHCR data, the review counts 5,817 Rohingya maritime departures between January and 8 August 2026 and 820 people reported dead or missing. The 2025 toll of 860 is described as about one in seven of those who tried the journey. Major incidents included the sinking of a boat from Bangladesh to Malaysia in April that killed at least 250 Rohingya and Bangladeshis, and two sinkings off Myanmar on 29 June and 8 July in which 260 and 280 people died or disappeared. UNHCR's November update says about 6,000 maritime movements were recorded on the South and South-East Asia route between January and September 2026, the highest for the first nine months of any year since systematic tracking began in 2022, with another estimated 10,700 land movements, most of them towards Bangladesh.

Finding 4: Aid cuts may be pushing more people onto boats

An essay in the review links departures to cuts in the camps. From 1 April 2026, it says, the monthly food allocation in Cox's Bazar was split into three tiers of $12, $10 and $7, with about 17% of refugees dropping to the lowest band. Between January and March 2026, 2,907 Rohingya left Bangladesh and Myanmar by boat, against 1,571 a year earlier, an 85% rise, and women and children were over half of those leaving. The authors are careful: these are small numbers against a camp population of more than a million, but they say it is "plausible" that withdrawing assistance is pushing more people onto boats. The review also notes that the 2026 Joint Response Plan was launched at $710.5 million, 26% less than the year before, and was 49% funded by mid-July.

What it means for the development sector

  • Safe migration programmes should treat irregular routes to Europe as part of the same problem as cheated labour migrants. If many people start on legal routes and end up in Libya, pre-departure information, recruitment monitoring and redress for failed contracts matter as much as border messaging. Devlens reported this week that 91% of cheated migrant workers in an OKUP study had no written contract.
  • Returnee and reintegration work may grow if the EU adopts its safe countries list and speeds up returns of Bangladeshis whose asylum claims fail.
  • Rohingya response partners have more evidence that ration cuts carry protection costs. The review's figures fit the UNHCR study linking aid cuts to a 28% rise in trafficking and recent rescues of Rohingya and local people in Teknaf. Counter-trafficking, community awareness and search-and-rescue advocacy need funding alongside food.
  • Donors should note that the same boats carry Bangladeshis as well as refugees, so host-community livelihoods are part of prevention.

Limits of the evidence

The review is mostly a compilation of other agencies' figures, and it does not give Bangladesh-specific numbers for 2026 asylum applications or returns. Its route data covers different periods (first half, first seven months, to 8 August), so figures cannot always be compared. Death counts at sea are estimates and likely incomplete. The link between ration cuts and departures is presented as plausible, not proven. The essays include the authors' views.

The bottom line

Fewer people are reaching Europe, but Bangladeshis remain the largest group making the crossing, often after a legal route failed them. In the Bay of Bengal, more Rohingya are taking to the sea as rations fall, and more are dying: almost as many in six months of 2026 as in all of 2025. Both trends point back to the same gaps that NGOs in Bangladesh already work on: fair recruitment, protection in the camps, and money to keep basic assistance going.

Sources

  • Mixed Migration Centre via ReliefWeb: Mixed Migration Review 2026: Migration in the age of polycrisis, 26 November 2026
  • UNHCR via ReliefWeb: Routes Monitor Key Updates, November 2026, 26 November 2026
